text:
Sunset is at 4:27, but with the clouds locked in you won't see much of it. It gets dark early and stays gray, with temperatures in the upper 30s and a damp chill, so grab the jacket for the evening. It's quiet through dinner. Around 1 or 2 in the morning, a few rain and snow showers move in, with hardly any measurable precipitation, and we bottom out near 35.

Saturday starts mostly dry, then the showers build in around 1 and run through about 6 or 7 in the evening. It's mostly rain with some wet snow flakes mixed in, and the high is near 40. Expect around a tenth of an inch, with a little more Saturday night as showers linger toward midnight. The lake may juice up a few showers late in the day. Nothing should stick in town, but the roads could be wet and slick in spots. If you want a dry window, do your errands or walk before noon.

Sunday is a bit milder, with a high near 42 and mostly cloudy skies. The forecasters keep a leftover shower or flurry around through early afternoon. The European model and a couple of others are wetter than that, so I'd bet on a damp morning and plan the dry stretch for later in the day.

Next week looks dry and brighter, warming into the 50s by midweek.

  1. Upslope snow showers will develop late tonight for the northwest facing slopes of the Adirondacks and Greens, with some possible Lake Champlain enhanced precipitation in the Champlain Valley late Saturday into Sunday.
  2. Conditions are expected to remain dry with a warming trend next week.

AFD DISCUSSION (the forecaster's full reasoning, same regional caveat; their temps are area-wide ranges):
KEY MESSAGE 1: Snow showers across southern Vermont will end this afternoon with a brief lull in precipitation for this evening. Clouds will remain as a reinforcing shortwave will shift south from Quebec later tonight into tomorrow. Wrap around moisture associated with the large upper level trough centered across our region will provide enough moisture to sustain upslope snow showers by tomorrow morning. As the shortwave dips into our area by tomorrow morning, blocked flow and orographic lift will lead to stratiform snow showers along our northwestern facing slopes in the northern Adirondacks and central and northern Greens. As the core of the shortwave passes through tomorrow early afternoon, our showery activity will turn more convective as marginal instability develops, allowing shower activity to survive the spine of the Greens into the eastern Greens, and survive the northwest slopes of the Adirondacks into the central northern Adirondacks. Snow showers will be strongest along the spine of the Greens with 3 to 5 inches of more powdery snow due to snow ratios around 10-15:1. Into the Adirondacks 2 to 4 inches is expected, with the highest amounts in the High Peaks and northern Franklin County in New York between US-11 and Saranac Lake. Snow levels look to initially hover around 1200ft agl, but dynamical cooling could lead to snow level lowering down towards 500ft, especially by tomorrow night in coordination with diurnal cooling. This could push some flakes into the eastern Champlain Valley where a few tenths of an inch of wet snow are possible. While snow amounts will be localized to the higher terrain, mountain passes, and untreated roads may become slick at times. Moreover, some localized power outages may be possible, but due to the drier character of the snow, impacts will be limited. As our snow turns more convective tomorrow afternoon into Saturday night, Lake Champlain streamers downstream of Lake Champlain look to develop as cold air aloft will be 10 degrees cooler than the current lake temperatures. Precipitation enhancement will be possible in the downstream regions of southern Chittenden and north and central Addison Counties. Precipitation types along this corridor will be mainly rain closest to the lake, with snow closer to the western slopes of the Greens, but dynamical cooling could push precipitation towards more snow closer to the lake at times. Accumulations look to be light as precipitable water will only be around 3 to 4 tenths of an inch. The position of any lake streamers are still somewhat uncertain, and will be dependent on the prevailing wind at the time, but it looks to be focused in an area between VT-22A and the spine of the Greens. Snow showers will lighten into Sunday, and taper off by Sunday evening, departing the highest summits of the Greens and NEK last. Solar heating, and gradual clearing will help to melt any snow in the lower elevations by Monday, with a warming and drying trend beginning early next week.
